# TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents

Aaron J. Li1, Weijia Xu2, Chandan Singh2, Zixiao Chen3, Jeevana Priya Inala2, Charlotte Siska3,
Acar Tamersoy3, Bin Yu1, Ion Stoica1, Michel Galley2, Jianfeng Gao2

1UC Berkeley   2Microsoft Research   3Microsoft Security

In the paper's SWE-Bench runs: 18.4–30.9% lower mean cost across five agent–model combinations, cheaper in all 30 repository × combination cells, and Pass@1 up in 4 of 5. Results

TokenEconomizer is a plugin for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, the **GitHub Copilot CLI** and **Pi**. It leaves the agent as it is, reads each finished session in a repository, and changes what the next sessions in that repository pay for: - **Micro-skills.** Environment facts your sessions keep rediscovering by failing at them -- that `pytest` is missing here and `python -m pytest` works, that the test runner wants labels without a `tests.` prefix -- are learned from recurring evidence and stated at the start of the next session. Learning them makes no model call. - **Tool pruning.** Tools that stay loaded but go unused, session after session (five in a row by default), are left out of the next sessions through the agent's own settings. By default this happens without asking you: the next session start says which tools were left out, and one command gives them back. Set `toolprune=propose` to approve each deny list yourself instead. - **Failure-loop intervention.** A turn that keeps repeating the same failing edit-and-test cycle, well past how long this repository's turns usually take, gets one redirect. If it is still stuck after that, the plugin tells you how to stop it; it never stops a turn itself. Each mechanism can be switched off or tuned on its own. The plugin's actions are announced in one line, every hook fails open, and by default it makes no model calls of its own. What it learns stays on your machine, under `~/.tokeneconomizer`. ## Results

The paper runs five agent–model combinations on the same 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, each repository's tasks in order and starting from no traces; costs include every call TokenEconomizer made. It was cheaper than default in each of the 30 repository × combination cells, by 5–40%, and the savings carried over to Web-Bench (16–21% lower) and to two security-auditing benchmarks where every task is a new repository (6–20% lower). The [project page](https://tokeneconomizer.github.io) has interactive charts, the per-repository numbers, and nine annotated runs; [`experiments/`](experiments/README.md) reruns the SWE-Bench and Web-Bench experiments. ## How it works Coding agents are built for task success, not for what a task costs, and every turn re-bills the agent's instructions, every loaded tool, and the conversation so far. Developers use the same agent on the same codebase over many tasks, so much of that cost recurs: the same environment facts rediscovered, the same unused tools re-sent, the same kind of failing loop. TokenEconomizer holds the agent fixed -- no change to its model, weights or code -- and treats a repository's stream of sessions as the unit to optimize: what finished sessions show about the repository shapes what later sessions are given, and anything the plugin spends is amortized over the stream. Four principles shape the mechanisms: - **Act through what the agent already reads.** Facts go into the context at session start and tools leave through the agent's own settings, so nothing depends on the agent adopting a new tool. - **Count cost as it is billed.** Most tokens in a session are cached re-reads, so cost is measured on a cache-aware basis, including any model calls the plugin makes. - **Keep task success.** Facts form only from recurring evidence, tools are pruned only after going unused, and the loop guard spares a turn that is still making progress. - **Recover from mistakes.** A fact a later session contradicts is retired, an applied deny list can be restored, and the guard only redirects and tells you: stopping a turn is your call. ## Quick start You need one of the four agents, signed in any way it supports, and Python 3.10 or newer on `PATH`. The plugin runs inside your agent's own sessions and never handles credentials, so any plan or login works, and it needs no API key of its own. ### Install Run the shell commands where the clone should stay: Claude Code, Codex and the Copilot CLI run the plugin from it. Then start the agent inside one of your repositories. **Claude Code** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git claude plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" claude plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `claude`, trust the folder (**Yes, I trust this folder**), and run `/tokeneconomizer:status`, allowing its script if asked. Once per machine, and again after Claude Code updates, run `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune refresh-catalog`. **Codex** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git codex plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" codex plugin add tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `codex`, choose **Trust and continue** for the folder, then at **Hooks need review** choose **Trust all and continue**; the hooks run from the next session on. Check with `$tokeneconomizer:status`. **Copilot CLI** ```sh git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git copilot plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer" copilot plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer ``` Start `copilot`, choose **Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions**, and run `/tokeneconomizer:status`, choosing **Yes** to run its script. Once per machine, and again after Copilot updates, run `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune refresh-catalog`. **Pi** ```sh pi install git:github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer ``` Start `pi` and run `/te status`. The status command prints a short status block. `refresh-catalog` records which tools a session loads, with no model call, so that tool pruning sees all of them. The marketplace path must be absolute: the Copilot CLI reads `./TokenEconomizer` as the name of a GitHub repository. To update: | Agent | Update | |---|---| | Claude Code, Copilot CLI | `git pull` in the clone | | Codex | `git pull` in the clone, then the `codex plugin add` line again | | Pi | `pi update --extensions` | Uninstalling, Copilot with your own model key, and troubleshooting are in **[`plugin/README.md`](plugin/README.md)**, which walks through each agent. ### Supported versions | Agent | Supported | Older versions | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | 2.1.300 to 2.1.307 | not supported | | Codex | 0.153.1 to 0.163.0 | not supported | | Copilot CLI | 1.0.83 to 1.0.102 | not supported | | Pi | 1.2.0 to 1.3.0 | 0.99.x: load the extension by path (below) | The commands above were checked on both ends of each range; later versions have not been checked. - **Codex before 0.141.0** does not run plugin hooks at all. - **Pi 0.99.x**: instead of `pi install`, clone the repository and start each session with `pi --extension /path/to/TokenEconomizer/plugin/pi/tokeneconomizer.ts`, using your clone's full path; `git pull` in the clone updates it. ### Everyday commands Work as usual; the plugin needs nothing from you. Its commands have the same names on every agent; only how you type them differs: | Agent | Type a command as | |---|---| | Claude Code, Copilot CLI | `/tokeneconomizer:` | | Codex | `$tokeneconomizer:` | | Pi | `/te ` | | a terminal, in the repository | `~/.tokeneconomizer/bin/te ` | | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `status` | what it learned and did here, and what your sessions cost | | `microskills` | the facts it injects, and those still forming | | `toolprune` | the tools it left out, and the evidence (not on Pi) | | `toolprune restore` | give them back; they will not be removed again | | `config` | every setting in effect | | `config set loopguard=off` | turn a mechanism off here; add `--global` for every repository | Inside an agent each command is one model turn; from a terminal it costs nothing. Every other command (`repos`, `doctor`, `config unset`, ...) and how each agent asks before running one: [Commands](plugin/README.md#commands). ## Settings The three mechanisms are `microskills`, `toolprune` and `loopguard`; each takes `on` or `off`, and each has numbers you can tune with the same `config set` command (in Claude Code's form here). Tool pruning is `auto` by default: once a tool has gone unused for `toolprune_evidence` sessions in a row (five), the plugin adds it to the deny list without asking, and it is left out from the next session on. It writes the list once your sessions in the repository have been idle for an hour (`toolprune_quiet_minutes`): a conversation resumed after its tools change writes its whole history to the prompt cache again instead of reading it, and after an idle hour that cache has expired anyway. With `toolprune=propose` the plugin only proposes the list, and nothing changes until you run `toolprune apply`. ```text /tokeneconomizer:config set microskills_max_facts=2 # inject at most two facts /tokeneconomizer:config set toolprune_evidence=10 # wait for ten unused sessions /tokeneconomizer:config set loopguard_nudges=2 # redirect twice before telling you ``` For one session only, set an environment variable when you start the agent: `TE_DISABLE=1 claude` turns the whole plugin off, and `TE_LOOPGUARD=off codex` (likewise `TE_MICROSKILLS`, `TE_TOOLPRUNE`) one mechanism. The paid helpers -- an LLM fact proposer and a judge for the loop guard -- are off unless you set `paid=true`; they run through your own agent's CLI, on the same plan or login as your sessions. Every setting, its default and its environment variable: [Settings](plugin/README.md#settings). ## What it does on each agent Micro-skills and the loop guard work the same way on every agent. Tool pruning acts through each agent's own settings, so what it can leave out differs: | Agent | Tool pruning leaves out | Written to | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | single tools | `.claude/settings.local.json` | | Codex | capability packages | `.codex/config.toml` | | Copilot CLI | whole MCP servers | `.github/copilot/settings.local.json` | | Pi | nothing: Pi loads four tools | — | Tool pruning writes only the entries it adds and never touches deny rules you wrote; a settings file it creates is kept out of git (`.git/info/exclude`). The next session start says what it left out. On Claude Code that line shows only in the detailed transcript (**Ctrl+O**), so `/tokeneconomizer:toolprune` is the place to check. `toolprune restore` removes the plugin's entries and no others, and what you give back stays back. If the plugin cannot edit a file safely (a `.codex/config.toml` your repository commits, a settings file that is not valid JSON, a path through a symlink), the list stays a proposal and the session start says why; `toolprune apply` tries again. How each agent's hooks and settings were verified to behave is in **[`docs/PLUGIN.md`](docs/PLUGIN.md)**, and how the package fits together in **[`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)**. ### When a turn gets stuck The first time a turn looks stuck, the loop guard adds a redirect to the model's context. If the turn is still stuck after that, it shows you one line, ending with how to stop the turn: > TokenEconomizer: this turn still looks stuck after a redirect (envelope, 12 tool calls). Press > Esc to interrupt it. It never stops a turn itself; whether to stop is up to you. Where the line shows, and how you stop, in the agent's terminal UI and in a headless run (`claude -p`, `codex exec`, `copilot -p`, `pi -p`): | Agent | Interactive: shown | Stop with | Headless: shown | Stop with | |---|---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | in Claude's reply | Esc | in the final reply | Ctrl+C | | Codex | in the conversation | Esc, then `/stop` | not shown | Ctrl+C | | Copilot CLI | in the conversation | Esc twice | on stdout | Ctrl+C | | Pi | as a notification | Esc | on stderr | Ctrl+C | - **Claude Code** keeps a plugin's own lines to its detailed transcript (Ctrl+O), so the plugin asks Claude to repeat the line; a model may word it differently or leave it out. - **Codex**: Esc interrupts the turn, but a command it started keeps running until `/stop`. `codex exec` prints no hook messages. - **Pi**: Ctrl+C ends a headless run, but a command it started runs on until it finishes. In a headless run nobody may be watching, so a flagged turn keeps running until it ends by itself or reaches the agent's own limits; `te status` counts the redirects and "still stuck" notices afterwards. ## Repository | | | |---|---| | [`tokeneconomizer/microskills`](tokeneconomizer/microskills/) | Micro-skill synthesis and injection: facts learned from finished sessions | | [`tokeneconomizer/toolprune`](tokeneconomizer/toolprune/) | Tool pruning: unused tools and Codex capability packages | | [`tokeneconomizer/loopguard`](tokeneconomizer/loopguard/) | Failure-loop intervention: the per-call guard and its per-repository envelope | | [`tokeneconomizer/trace`](tokeneconomizer/trace/) | Each agent's session log, read into one shape | | [`tokeneconomizer/plugin`](tokeneconomizer/plugin/) | The runtime the hooks and the `te` command run | | [`plugin`](plugin/) | The installable plugin: manifests, hook files, launchers, slash commands, the Pi extension | | [`experiments`](experiments/) | The harness, launchers and task sets behind the paper's results | | [`docs`](docs/) | `PLUGIN.md` (design, verified agent behavior) and `ARCHITECTURE.md` (how the package fits together) | | [`tests`](tests/) | Offline tests for the package and the plugin | The package is standard-library only. Run the tests with `python -m pytest tests` (add `experiments/tests` for the benchmark side), and build a self-contained plugin bundle with `python3 scripts/build_plugin.py --out dist/marketplace`. ## Reproducing the experiments The code behind the paper's results -- a harness that runs Claude Code, Codex and the Copilot CLI on SWE-Bench and Web-Bench, the launchers, and the evaluated task sets -- is in **[`experiments/`](experiments/README.md)**, whose README gives the setup and one command per result. [build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "tokeneconomizer"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Experience-driven black-box cost control for coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Pi), as a plugin."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
license = { text = "Apache-2.0" }
authors = [{ name = "TokenEconomizer authors" }]
keywords = ["llm-agents", "cost-optimization", "swe-bench", "token-economy"]

# The package is STDLIB-ONLY: the three mechanisms, the trace reader, the ledger and the plugin
# runtime import nothing outside the standard library, so it runs on any Python >=3.10 with zero
# install-time dependencies.
dependencies = []

[project.scripts]
# The plugin's command line (status, microskills, toolprune, config, ...). The plugin ships its
# own launcher (plugin/scripts/te) and does not need the package installed.
te = "tokeneconomizer.plugin.cli:main"

[project.optional-dependencies]
# Test suite is offline (no Docker / no datasets).
test = ["pytest>=7.0"]
# The reference task-execution harness under experiments/te_harness/ (see
# experiments/README.md). It adds no
# PyPI dependency -- it is stdlib-only at import time and the official SWE-bench grader is
# imported lazily from a checkout named by TE_SWEBENCH_REPO -- so this extra installs
# nothing. It exists to give "I intend to run the harness" a name, since what the harness
# actually needs cannot come from pip: Docker, an agent CLI on PATH, an API key, the
# benchmark images, and for Web-Bench a built Rush monorepo.
harness = []
# The repo-map external baseline (experiments/te_bench/baselines/repomap.py) generates aider's
# token-budgeted map on the HOST -- the task container's Python is pinned to the issue's
# era and cannot run a modern tree-sitter stack. This is the ONLY baseline with a host
# dependency: rtk ships a static binary and Serena installs itself in-container.
#
# It stays an EXTRA: aider is imported inside `preflight()`, and the generator both the
# baseline and the plugin's opt-in map run (tokeneconomizer/plugin/repomap_gen.py) is a subprocess
# that nothing imports, so `import tokeneconomizer` keeps its zero-dependency guarantee. A
# machine that will never make a repo map never needs aider installed.
baselines = ["aider-chat>=0.60"]

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
# The package ONLY. The reproduction code (experiments/, including te_harness and te_bench) is
# deliberately not distributed: `import tokeneconomizer` must not be able to reach Docker or a
# benchmark harness, and excluding it here is what makes that structural.
include = ["tokeneconomizer*"]
exclude = ["experiments*", "te_harness*", "tests*", "scripts*"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests", "experiments/tests"]
addopts = "-q"

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
# The Claude Code tool-description snapshot the catalog reader joins against.
tokeneconomizer = ["trace/*.json"]

# GoiBERT: Compact Vietnamese Language Models via Two-Stage Knowledge Distillation **Quang Anh Kiet Tran**1\* · **Nam Anh Tran**2\* · **Manh Hung Trinh**3 · **Thanh Danh Le**2 · **Khang Nhat Hoang Vo**4 · **Huynh Dai Nhan Tran**5 1UIT, VNU-HCM   2IU, VNU-HCM   3University of Eastern Finland   4MBZUAI   5University of Jyväskylä \*Equal contribution Correspondence: [huynh.d.n.tran@jyu.fi](mailto:huynh.d.n.tran@jyu.fi) [🤗 GoiBERT-base](https://huggingface.co/2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-S) · [🤗 GoiBERT-large](https://huggingface.co/2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-M) · [Corpus card](release/goi-corpus-v2/README.md)
--- ## Overview Vietnamese pre-trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the strongest ones are either large models with multilingual vocabularies or depend on an external word segmenter, which makes them costly to deploy. **GoiBERT** is a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders, with **26.4M** and **49.4M** parameters, that read **raw text with no word segmentation**. GoiBERT learns from two teachers that complement each other, and each teacher is used in the stage where its strengths matter: 1. **General distillation.** [BamiBERT](https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT) uses the same tokenizer as GoiBERT. It teaches general-purpose representations through layer-wise hidden-state and attention transfer on unlabeled text. 2. **Out-of-fold task distillation.** CafeBERT (559M) is much larger and uses a different tokenizer. It provides task-level soft labels at the output, where the tokenizer mismatch does not matter. These labels are produced *out of fold*, so no teacher ever labels an example it was trained on. Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA), natural language inference (NLI) and named entity recognition (NER): - **GoiBERT-large** has the highest average score among non-teacher models. It has fewer than half of BamiBERT's parameters and twice its GPU throughput. - **GoiBERT-base** reaches 99% of BamiBERT's average score with a quarter of its parameters and 3.5× its throughput.

The GoiBERT training pipeline. (1) The student matches the hidden states and attention maps of a frozen BamiBERT on unlabeled text. (2) Five CafeBERT teachers, each fine-tuned on four folds, label the held-out fold. (3) The distilled backbone is fine-tuned on gold labels and CafeBERT soft labels, with layer-wise learning-rate decay.

## Models | Model (paper name) | Hub ID | Layers | Hidden | Heads | FFN | Params | Embedding share | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | GoiBERT-base | [`2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-S`](https://huggingface.co/2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-S) | 10 | 384 | 6 | 1,536 | 26.4M | 33% | | GoiBERT-large | [`2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-M`](https://huggingface.co/2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-M) | 12 | 512 | 8 | 2,048 | 49.4M | 23% | Both models follow the RoBERTa encoder architecture. They use BamiBERT's 20,481-token tokenizer and 64-dimensional attention heads. The released checkpoints are the backbone encoders after general distillation (Stage 1) and have no task head. Distillation used sequences of at most 256 tokens, so we recommend `max_length=256`. ### Quick start ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-M") model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("2HeartsVN/GoiBERT-M") inputs = tokenizer("Sản phẩm dùng tốt, giao hàng nhanh.", return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=256) hidden = model(**inputs).last_hidden_state # (1, seq_len, 512) ``` ## Method ### Compact architecture and initialization The small vocabulary is itself a source of efficiency. Embeddings make up only 33% (base) and 23% (large) of the parameters, compared with 46% for CafeBERT and 69% for XLM-R. GoiBERT-large's word embeddings are initialized by projecting BamiBERT's 768-dimensional embedding matrix onto its 512 leading principal components, then rescaling to the student's initialization scale. Transformer blocks are initialized randomly. ### Stage 1: general distillation The student matches a frozen BamiBERT on unlabeled text. A trainable linear projection $P^v_\ell$ maps each student layer into the 768-dimensional teacher space, and the error is computed only over non-padding positions: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{hid}} = \frac{1}{L_v+1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{L_v} \text{MSE}_{\text{nonpad}}\big(P^v_\ell(H^v_\ell),\, H^B_{\pi_v(\ell)}\big)$$ The two models have different numbers of heads, so we match **head-averaged** post-softmax attention maps $\bar A^m_\ell = \frac{1}{a_m}\sum_h A^m_{\ell,h}$: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{att}} = \frac{1}{L_v}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_v} \text{MSE}\big(\bar A^v_\ell,\, \bar A^B_{\pi_v(\ell)}\big), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{GD}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{hid}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{att}}$$ **Layer mapping.** For GoiBERT-large, $\pi_{\text{large}}$ is the identity (12 ↔ 12 layers). For GoiBERT-base, $\pi_{\text{base}}(0)=0$ aligns the embedding outputs, and student layers 1–10 learn from teacher layers $(1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12)$. Teacher layers 3 and 9 are skipped, and depth order is preserved. ### Stage 2: out-of-fold task distillation A 559M-parameter teacher fits its own training examples closely, so its predictions on them are nearly one-hot. We therefore cross-fit in the spirit of stacked generalization. The training set is split into five folds, one CafeBERT is fine-tuned on each set of four folds, and it predicts only the held-out fold. The student is trained with $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}} = \alpha\,\text{CE}\big(y, p_S^{(1)}\big) + (1-\alpha)\,T^2\,\text{KL}\big(p_C^{(T)} \,\|\, p_S^{(T)}\big), \qquad \alpha = 0.5,\; T = 2.$$ The loss is applied once per example for classification and NLI, and independently to each aspect slot for ABSA. For NER, both models' predictions are aligned to the first subword of each original syllable. **Layer-wise learning-rate decay (LLRD).** Layer $\ell$ uses $\eta_\ell = \eta\,\gamma^{L_v-\ell}$ with $\gamma = 0.8$. The embeddings use $\eta\gamma^{L_v}$ and the task head uses $\eta$. ## Experimental Setup ### Benchmarks We keep the official training, validation and test splits of every dataset. | Task | Family | Domain | Metrics | Primary metric | |---|---|---|---|---| | UIT-VSFC Sentiment | Classification | Student feedback | Acc., M-F1 | M-F1 | | UIT-VSFC Topic | Classification | Student feedback | Acc., M-F1 | M-F1 | | ViSpamReviews (4-class) | Classification | E-commerce reviews | Acc., M-F1 | M-F1 | | UIT-ViSFD | ABSA | Smartphone reviews | Det., Pair | Pair | | UIT-ABSA Restaurant | ABSA | Restaurant reviews | Det., Pair | Pair | | UIT-ABSA Hotel | ABSA | Hotel reviews | Det., Pair | Pair | | ViNLI (`presencesw/vinli_4_label`) | NLI | News (open domain) | Acc., M-F1 | M-F1 | | PhoNER_COVID19 | NER | COVID-19 news | Ent. ## Which variant should I use? - **GoiBERT-large** is the better default when accuracy matters and a GPU is available. It is the strongest non-teacher model on average and roughly matches CafeBERT on classification and ABSA, at half of BamiBERT's serving cost. - **GoiBERT-base** suits CPU-only inference, edge devices or high-throughput batch labeling.  Abstract 
    
 Vietnamese pre-trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the
strongest ones are large, multilingual-vocabulary models or depend on
external word segmentation, which makes them costly to deploy.
We present  GoiBERT , a family of two compact Vietnamese
encoders with 26M and 49M parameters that operate directly on raw text.
GoiBERT learns from two complementary teachers.
A same-tokenizer Vietnamese encoder first teaches general-purpose
representations.
A much larger teacher then provides task-level guidance through soft
labels that are generated without ever labeling its own training data.
Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect-based
sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and named entity
recognition, GoiBERT-large achieves the highest average score among
non-teacher models.
It does so with fewer than half the parameters of the strongest compact
baseline and twice its throughput.
GoiBERT-base retains 99% of that baseline’s performance at a quarter
of its size.
Our analysis shows that compression is nearly lossless for sentiment
and classification tasks but remains costly for inference and entity
recognition, which points to clear directions for future work. Our code and models are available at:  https://github.com/Nhantran65/GoiBERT.git 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 1  Introduction 

 
 Pre-trained Transformer encoders remain the workhorse of practical language
understanding: they power text classification, sentiment analysis,
information extraction, and retrieval in production systems where
generative large language models are too slow or too costly to serve
 Devlin et al. (2019) ;  Liu et al. (2019b) ;  Conneau et al. (2020) ;  Warner et al. (2025) .
Vietnamese NLP has followed this trajectory closely, moving from
multilingual encoders to a growing family of monolingual models such as
PhoBERT, ViDeBERTa, ViSoBERT, and the recent BamiBERT, as well as
CafeBERT, a large XLM-R model further adapted to Vietnamese
 Nguyen and Tuan Nguyen (2020) ;  Tran et al. (2023) ;  Nguyen et al. (2023b) ;  Nguyen et al. (2026) ;  Do et al. (2024) . 
 
 
 These models have steadily raised the bar on Vietnamese benchmarks, but
each comes with a deployment cost.
The strongest model, CafeBERT, has 559M parameters, and more than
45% of them sit in its multilingual embedding matrix.
PhoBERT expects word-segmented input and therefore needs an external
segmenter at inference time  Vu et al. (2018) .
ViSoBERT targets social-media text, and even the most compact strong
monolingual baseline, BamiBERT, uses a 102M-parameter encoder.
For the many Vietnamese applications that run on CPUs, small GPUs, or
under tight latency budgets, the field still lacks a  compact ,
 segmentation-free  encoder that holds up across diverse tasks. 
 
 
 Figure 1:  Average score over eight Vietnamese benchmarks versus model
size. Both GoiBERT variants lie on the accuracy–efficiency frontier
of non-teacher models: GoiBERT-large has the highest average with
less than half of BamiBERT’s parameters, and GoiBERT-base stays close
with about a quarter of them. 
 
 
 Knowledge distillation (KD) is the standard tool for closing this gap in
English, where compact students such as DistilBERT, TinyBERT, MobileBERT,
and MiniLM retain most of their teachers’ accuracy at a fraction of their
cost  Hinton et al. (2015) ;  Sanh et al. (2019) ;  Jiao et al. (2020) ;  Sun et al. (2020) ;  Wang et al. (2020) .
Transferring these recipes to Vietnamese, however, raises a design
question that English work rarely faces:  which teacher should the
student learn from? 
The most accurate Vietnamese teacher (CafeBERT) uses a large
multilingual vocabulary that does not match any compact Vietnamese
tokenizer.
This rules out the token-level hidden-state and attention matching
that makes TinyBERT-style general distillation effective.
A same-tokenizer teacher (BamiBERT) supports such matching but is
itself weaker on several tasks.
To our knowledge, no prior work has studied how to combine these
complementary signals for Vietnamese, and Vietnamese compact encoders
have not been evaluated systematically for both accuracy and deployment
cost. 
 
 
 We present  GoiBERT , a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders:
GoiBERT-base (26.4M parameters) and GoiBERT-large (49.4M parameters).
Our key idea is to  assign each teacher to the stage where its
strengths matter .
In the first stage, BamiBERT, which shares GoiBERT’s tokenizer, teaches
general-purpose representations through layer-wise hidden-state and
attention transfer on unlabeled text.
In the second stage, CafeBERT supplies task-specific soft labels at the
output level, where tokenizer mismatch is irrelevant.
We produce these labels  out of fold , so that no teacher ever
labels an example it was trained on.
As Figure  1  shows, the resulting students move the
accuracy–efficiency frontier for Vietnamese.
GoiBERT-large achieves the best average score among non-teacher models
with fewer than half of BamiBERT’s parameters and twice its GPU
throughput.
GoiBERT-base retains 99% of BamiBERT’s average score with a quarter of
its parameters and 3.5 × \times  its throughput. 
 
 
 Our contributions are threefold: 
 
 •  
 
 Models.  We release GoiBERT-base and GoiBERT-large,
compact Vietnamese encoders that process raw text without word
segmentation and offer two complementary accuracy–efficiency
operating points. 
 
 •  
 
 Method.  We propose a two-teacher, two-stage
distillation framework. It pairs representation transfer from a
tokenizer-compatible teacher with out-of-fold, output-level
supervision from a stronger cross-tokenizer teacher, and it combines
this with teacher-derived embedding initialization and layer-wise
learning-rate decay. 
 
 •  
 
 Analysis.  We evaluate on eight benchmarks (15 metrics,
three seeds) and measure parameters, FLOPs, throughput, memory, and
CPU latency. Ablations and per-task analysis show where compression
is nearly free (sentiment, ABSA, topic, and spam classification) and
where it still costs accuracy (NLI and NER). 
 
 
 
 
 
 2  Related Work 

 
 Our work draws on three lines of research: Vietnamese pre-trained
encoders, knowledge distillation for compact Transformers, and
efficient language-specific models. 
 
 
 Vietnamese pre-trained encoders. 

 
 Vietnamese NLP has moved from multilingual encoders such as XLM-R
 Conneau et al. (2020)  to a growing family of monolingual models.
After early BERT and ELECTRA adaptations  Bui et al. (2020) ,
PhoBERT set strong baselines but requires word-segmented input from an
external segmenter  Nguyen and Tuan Nguyen (2020) ;  Vu et al. (2018) .
This design choice reflects a property of the language: Vietnamese is
written as space-separated syllables, and many words span several of
them, so a model must either receive word boundaries explicitly or learn
them from raw text.
Later models changed the pre-training objective (ViDeBERTa;
 Tran et al., 2023 ) or the target domain (ViSoBERT for social
media and ViHealthBERT for health;
 Nguyen et al., 2023b ;  Minh et al., 2022 ).
Others added linguistic inductive bias: HuTieuBERT injects
morpheme-boundary information into a pre-trained encoder to reflect the
isolating structure of Vietnamese  Dinh et al. (2026) .
BamiBERT is a recent general-purpose raw-text encoder
 Nguyen et al. (2026) , while CafeBERT continues pre-training
XLM-R-large on Vietnamese and leads the VLUE benchmark
 Do et al. (2024) .
Generative models such as ViT5, BARTpho, and PhoGPT
 Phan et al. (2022) ;  Tran et al. (2022) ;  Nguyen et al. (2023a)  target text
generation and are complementary to encoders, which remain the
cost-effective choice for understanding tasks.
Benchmarks such as VLUE and ViGLUE  Do et al. (2024) ;  Tran et al. (2024) 
have made these models comparable, but only in terms of accuracy.
Similar efforts for other medium-resource languages, such as
Indonesian, Indic languages, Bangla, and Thai, have likewise focused on
full-size models
 Wilie et al. (2020) ;  Kakwani et al. (2020) ;  Bhattacharjee et al. (2022) ;  Lowphansirikul et al. (2021) .
This line of work has therefore steadily raised accuracy while model
sizes have stayed around or above 100M parameters.
GoiBERT asks the complementary question of how much of that accuracy
can be retained at a fraction of the cost. 
 
 
 
 Knowledge distillation for compact encoders. 

 
 Knowledge distillation (KD) trains a small student to mimic the
softened predictions of a larger teacher  Hinton et al. (2015) .
For BERT-style encoders, KD has been extended from output logits to
intermediate signals.
PKD and DistilBERT match intermediate layers or initialize the student
from the teacher  Sun et al. (2019b) ;  Sanh et al. (2019) , MobileBERT
transfers layer-wise features  Sun et al. (2020) , and MiniLM
transfers self-attention distributions
 Wang et al. (2020) ;  Wang et al. (2021) .
TinyBERT  Jiao et al. (2020)  combines these signals into the
two-stage scheme we build on: general distillation of hidden states and
attention on unlabeled text, followed by task-specific distillation.
The general stage lets a compact student acquire broad language
knowledge without being pre-trained from scratch, and the task stage
then specializes it with the teacher’s predictions.
Comparative studies further show that pre-training the student
 Turc et al. (2019)  and the choice of distillation objective
 Udagawa et al. (2023)  strongly affect the final model.
Two findings from this literature shape our design.
First, a teacher much larger than its student can transfer poorly
 Cho and Hariharan (2019) ;  Mirzadeh et al. (2020) , which favors a mid-sized teacher
for representation transfer.
Second, soft labels partly act as a regularizer, so a student can match
or even surpass its teacher  Furlanello et al. (2018) ;  Yuan et al. (2020) .
Existing two-stage methods use a single teacher in both stages, and
multi-teacher approaches combine several teachers into one supervision
signal  Liu et al. (2019a) ;  Yuan et al. (2021) ;  Avram et al. (2022) .
When teacher and student vocabularies differ, distillation must
additionally align them  Boizard et al. (2025) ;  Zhang et al. (2024) .
GoiBERT sidesteps this problem by giving each teacher its own stage.
A same-tokenizer teacher supervises representations, and a
cross-tokenizer teacher supervises only task outputs, whose soft labels
we generate out of fold in the spirit of stacked generalization
 Wolpert (1992) . 
 
 
 
 Efficient language-specific encoders. 

 
 A complementary line of work builds compact models for a single
language.
One route starts from multilingual models, either trimming their
vocabulary  Abdaoui et al. (2020) ;  Ushio et al. (2023)  or distilling
them into language-specific students
 Mukherjee and Hassan Awadallah (2020) ;  Ansell et al. (2023) ;  Cruz (2025) .
Another distills monolingual teachers, as in DistilCamemBERT for French
 Delestre and Amar (2022) .
In both cases, the student typically inherits its vocabulary and its
supervision from the same single teacher.
GoiBERT combines the two routes.
Its tokenizer and initial embeddings come from a monolingual teacher,
in line with evidence that initializing small models from larger ones
helps  Samragh et al. (2023) ;  Xu et al. (2024) .
Its task supervision comes from a teacher of multilingual origin.
Pruning  Sanh et al. (2020) ;  Xia et al. (2022) , quantization
 Kim et al. (2021) , and parameter sharing  Lan et al. (2020)  are
orthogonal and can be applied on top of
GoiBERT.
Finally, parameter counts and FLOPs can misrepresent real speed
 Dehghani et al. (2022) .
Following recent efficiency-focused encoders such as ModernBERT
 Warner et al. (2025) , we therefore report measured throughput,
memory, and latency alongside predictive accuracy. 
 
 
 
 
 3  GoiBERT 

 
 Figure 2:  Overview of the GoiBERT training pipeline.
 (1)  General distillation: the student matches the hidden
states and attention maps of a frozen BamiBERT, which shares its
tokenizer, on unlabeled Vietnamese text.
 (2)  Out-of-fold soft labels: five CafeBERT teachers, each
fine-tuned on four folds, label the held-out fold, so that no
example is labeled by a teacher that saw it.
 (3)  Task fine-tuning: the distilled backbone is trained on
gold labels and CafeBERT soft labels with layer-wise learning-rate
decay. 
 
 
 GoiBERT is designed around one observation.
The two strongest available teachers offer  different kinds  of
knowledge, and each kind can only be transferred at a particular
granularity.
BamiBERT tokenizes text exactly as GoiBERT does, so its token-level
hidden states and attention maps can be matched position by position.
CafeBERT is considerably more accurate on several tasks, but its
250K-entry multilingual vocabulary segments the same sentence
differently, so its knowledge can only be transferred cleanly through
sequence- or word-level predictions.
GoiBERT therefore uses BamiBERT for  task-agnostic representation
transfer  and CafeBERT for  task-specific output supervision 
(Figure  2 ), extending the two-stage design of
TinyBERT  Jiao et al. (2020)  to two heterogeneous teachers with complementary roles. 
 
 
 3.1  Compact Architecture 

 
 GoiBERT follows the RoBERTa encoder architecture  Liu et al. (2019b) 
and reuses BamiBERT’s 20,481-token vocabulary and tokenizer, so it
processes raw Vietnamese text without word segmentation.
 GoiBERT-base  has 10 Transformer layers, hidden size 384,
6 attention heads, and a 1,536-dimensional feed-forward layer
(26.4M parameters).
 GoiBERT-large  has 12 layers, hidden size 512, 8 heads, and a
2,048-dimensional feed-forward layer (49.4M parameters).
Both use 64-dimensional attention heads, as BamiBERT does.
The compact vocabulary is itself a source of efficiency.
Embeddings account for only 33% and 23% of the parameters of
GoiBERT-base and GoiBERT-large, respectively, compared with 46% for
CafeBERT and 69% for XLM-R (Table  5 ).
To inherit lexical knowledge from the teacher, we initialize
GoiBERT-large’s word embeddings by projecting BamiBERT’s 768-dimensional
embedding matrix onto its 512 leading principal components and
rescaling to the student’s initialization scale.
Transformer blocks are initialized randomly.

 4  Experimental Setup 

 
 Benchmarks. 

 
 We evaluate on eight Vietnamese tasks that span four task families and
several domains (Appendix Table  7 ).
 Text classification  covers sentiment and topic classification of
student feedback in UIT-VSFC  Nguyen et al. (2018)  and four-class
spam detection of e-commerce reviews in ViSpamReviews

 Aspect-based sentiment analysis  (ABSA) covers smartphone reviews

 Natural language inference  (NLI) uses ViNLI

 Named entity recognition  (NER) uses PhoNER_COVID19

We keep the official training, validation, and test splits. 
 
 
 
 Metrics. 

 
 Classification and NLI are scored with accuracy and macro-F1, and ABSA
with aspect-detection F1 and end-to-end aspect–sentiment pair
micro-F1. NER is scored with strict entity-level F1.
This yields 15 metrics in total (Appendix  E ).
In the main text we report one primary metric per task: macro-F1 for
classification and NLI, pair F1 for ABSA, and entity F1 for NER.
All locally trained models are averaged over three fine-tuning seeds
(42, 43, 44)  Dodge et al. (2020) . 
 
 
 
 Baselines. 

 
 We compare against the monolingual encoders PhoBERT-base-v2
 Nguyen and Tuan Nguyen (2020) , ViSoBERT  Nguyen et al. (2023b) , and
BamiBERT  Nguyen et al. (2026) ; the multilingual XLM-R-base

our task teacher.
BamiBERT is our principal comparison because it is the most recent
compact Vietnamese encoder and our Stage 1 teacher.
We re-run it under the same downstream protocol as GoiBERT, with its
learning rate tuned on validation data and standard cross-entropy
fine-tuning.
ViDeBERTa  Tran et al. (2023)  results are reported in
Appendix  E .

 General distillation uses 328.6M tokens of clean, unlabeled Vietnamese
text from HPLT 3.0  Oepen et al. (2026) , Wikipedia, and the
 training  splits of selected benchmarks.
To prevent leakage, we remove every passage that matches validation or
test content under exact matching or 13-gram overlap

 Implementation. 

 
 General distillation runs for 120K steps (batch 32, sequence length
256) with AdamW, learning rate  10 − 4 10^{-4} , and linear decay, on a single
NVIDIA L40S GPU in bfloat16.
Task fine-tuning runs for 30 epochs with batch size 32.
Learning rates and checkpoints are selected on validation data only.
Efficiency is measured on the encoder alone.
GPU throughput and peak memory are measured on an L40S (bf16, batch 32,
length 256), and CPU latency on a single 128-token input with eight
threads (fp32).
The same protocol is applied to every model.

rather than a lack of supervision.
First, ViNLI is the task most sensitive to model size within the GoiBERT
family: the base–large gap is 2.66 points, compared with 0.89 on

informative, but a 12-layer, 512-dimensional
student cannot fully absorb the cross-sentence reasoning that the
24-layer, 1024-dimensional teacher performs.
For NER, two factors may contribute.
Entity F1 is already high (above 92 for all models), leaving little
room for distillation to help.
In addition, aligning supervision to the first subword of each syllable
discards the multi-syllable word boundaries that PhoBERT receives from
its segmenter, and these boundaries frequently coincide with entity
boundaries in Vietnamese.
Distillation objectives tailored to inference and span structure are a
natural next step.

GoiBERT-base needs 4.7 × \times  fewer FLOPs than BamiBERT but runs
only 3.5 × \times  faster on GPU and 2.2 × \times  faster on CPU.
At small widths, memory-bound operations such as layer normalization
and embedding lookups, together with fixed per-call overhead, take up a
growing share of runtime.
This echoes the warning that FLOPs and parameter counts are imperfect
proxies for real efficiency  Dehghani et al. (2022) .
It also makes GoiBERT-large, whose 2.2 × \times  FLOP reduction
translates almost fully into a 2.0 × \times  GPU speed-up, the more
balanced choice when accuracy matters.
GoiBERT-base is preferable for CPU-only or memory-constrained serving. 
 
 
 Where do the parameters go? 

 
 Table  5  breaks each model’s size into embedding and
encoder parameters, which explains much of the efficiency picture.
Multilingual vocabularies impose a large fixed cost:
69% of XLM-R-base and 46% of CafeBERT are embeddings, and these
parameters add memory without adding per-token computation.
BamiBERT’s compact 20K-token vocabulary already avoids most of this
cost, so GoiBERT’s savings over BamiBERT come mainly from the encoder:
37.8M encoder parameters for GoiBERT-large and 17.7M for GoiBERT-base,
compared with 85.1M.
Consequently, the encoder is where further compression should target,
for example through pruning or quantization
 Xia et al. (2022) ;  Kim et al. (2021) , whereas for multilingual models
vocabulary trimming is the more natural first step
 Abdaoui et al. (2020) ;  Ushio et al. (2023) . 
 
 
 
 Which variant should practitioners use? 

 
 The two variants serve different deployment regimes.
When accuracy is the priority and a GPU is available, GoiBERT-large is
the better default.
It is the strongest non-teacher model on average, roughly matches
CafeBERT on classification and ABSA, and still halves BamiBERT’s
serving cost.
When the budget is tight, such as CPU-only inference, edge devices, or
high-throughput batch labeling, GoiBERT-base offers the lowest latency
and memory with an average loss of only 1.1 points relative to
GoiBERT-large.
For NLI-heavy applications, a larger encoder remains preferable.

 6  Conclusion 

 
 We introduced GoiBERT, a family of compact, segmentation-free
Vietnamese encoders trained by two-stage distillation from two
complementary teachers.
A tokenizer-compatible teacher transfers general representations, and a
much larger cross-tokenizer teacher supplies out-of-fold task
supervision.
GoiBERT-large (49.4M parameters) achieves the best average score among
non-teacher models across eight benchmarks, doubles the GPU throughput
of BamiBERT, and comes within half a point of its 559M-parameter teacher
outside NLI.
GoiBERT-base (26.4M) retains 99% of BamiBERT’s average with a quarter
of its parameters.
Our analysis shows that compression is nearly free for classification
and ABSA but still costly for inference and entity recognition.
This two-teacher recipe should also transfer to other languages whose
strongest models are multilingual.
Future work will target NLI- and NER-specific distillation, longer
contexts, unseen domains, and quantization. 
 
 
 
 Limitations 

 
 Our comparison with BamiBERT is not a pure architecture comparison.
GoiBERT also benefits from CafeBERT distillation, layer-wise
learning-rate decay, and a general-distillation corpus that includes
benchmark  training  text, while our BamiBERT re-run uses plain
cross-entropy fine-tuning. We should also be upfront that we decided to build the larger variant after looking at earlier test results, so test feedback partly shaped how the models were developed. 
 
 
 On the statistical side, we ran general distillation only once.
The seed ranges we report therefore reflect fine-tuning variability
alone, and they are not confidence intervals or significance tests.
Our ablations cover just three tasks and add components one at a time, so they do not fully separate how the components interact.
The 8- and 15-metric averages are handy summaries, but they mix metrics that mean different things. 
 
 
 There are also things we did not test. We distill on sequences of at most 256 tokens, so we do not know how GoiBERT handles long inputs, and none of our benchmarks probe unseen domains or dialectal variation. Our efficiency numbers cover encoder inference on the hardware we used. They leave out tokenization, task heads, and the cost of training five out-of-fold CafeBERT teachers for each task, which is substantial even though it is paid only once. 
 
 
 
 Ethics Statement 

 
 GoiBERT is trained on publicly available text and benchmarks, so it can pick up social biases from web data and from its teachers.
We have not audited the models for such biases, and we encourage
anyone deploying them in sensitive settings to check first.
On the positive side, smaller models make Vietnamese NLP cheaper to run and accessible on more modest hardware.

 Appendix A  Architecture and Initialization 

 
 Figure  4  provides a layer-level view of
the GoiBERT encoder family.
The model configurations are summarized in § 3.1 ; here we
provide the additional implementation details omitted from the main paper. 
 
 
 For GoiBERT-large, the word embeddings are initialized from BamiBERT’s
768-dimensional embedding matrix using principal component analysis
(PCA), retaining the leading 512 components.
The projected embeddings are normalized and rescaled to match the
standard deviation of the student’s embedding initialization.
Transformer blocks are initialized randomly.

embeddings; general distillation uses sequences of at most 256 tokens.

 Appendix D  Training and Measurement Details 

 
 General distillation is run for 120,000 optimization steps with batch
size 32 and sequence length 256.
We use AdamW with learning rate  10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay  0.01 0.01 ,
1,000 warmup steps, and linear learning-rate decay.
This stage uses seed 42 and bfloat16 precision on one NVIDIA L40S GPU. 
 
 
 For downstream tasks, both GoiBERT variants are fine-tuned for
30 epochs with batch size 32 using AdamW, weight decay  0.01 0.01 , and
10% warmup.
The base learning rate is  10 − 5 10^{-5}  for the two UIT-VSFC tasks,
 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5}  for ViSpamReviews, and  10 − 4 10^{-4}  for the remaining
tasks.
GoiBERT additionally uses the layer-wise decay in
Eq.  6 .
For the rerun BamiBERT baseline, the learning rate is selected from
 { 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 , 5 × 10 − 5 } \{10^{-5},2\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5}\}  using validation
performance; BamiBERT is trained with cross-entropy only. 
 
 
 Model selection is based exclusively on validation data.
Reported local test results are averaged over fine-tuning seeds
42, 43, and 44. 
 
 
 Efficiency measurements use the encoder only.
GPU throughput and peak VRAM are measured on an NVIDIA L40S using
bfloat16 and scaled-dot-product attention at batch size 32 and sequence
length 256.
CPU latency is measured in float32 with eight CPU threads for a single
128-token input.
Timing measurements use repeated forward passes after warm-up; the
same measurement protocol is applied to all compared encoders.
